section_candidates.excerpt: from precisely-dated late Palaeocene limestones from the former northern margin of the Indian subcontinent, now in Tibet, between the major Himalayan thrusts and the India- Tibet suture zone. Geology As in Jamaica the geology of Hispaniola is complex and not very well known. BUTTERLIN (1956) and WEYL (1966) have described its general aspects and BOWIN (1966)-has mapped in some detail Late Cretaceous and Eocene rocks in Central Dominican Republic. More recently MACDONALD and MELSON (1969) described the Miocene intrusives and Recent lavas in Eastern Dominican Republic. In a paleomagnetic sampling reconnaissance conducted in 1972 a number ofintru- sives and lavas were sampled in the Dominican Republic and Haiti. te Miocene andesite are ambiguous. Table 1 shows that AF treatment has separated the directions of magnetization into two distinct groups and it is not clear which of the two directions is primary. The mean for YA and YB corre- sponds to an approximate reversal of the present-day field, while that for YC and YD agrees closely with the direction obtained from Miocene lavas on Jamacia (GuJA and VINCENZ, 1977), see also Fig. 3. It is conceivable that the mild regional hydrothermal alteration of the andesite may have been late post-formational and could have affected the original cooling TRM. The alteration is indicated by granulation of titanomagnetite without affecting the ilmenite lamellae and it is usually accepted that this type of change is associated with reheating to a maximum of about 200~ (ADE- HALL et al., 1971). This could have imposed a partial TRM or a CRM of more recent origin. The stability of this secondary remanence resulting from an oxidation process may be higher than that of the primary remanence and AF treatment might be ineffec- tive in removing it. In such a case the 'clean' NRM would still differ in direction from the original cooling TRM. It is, however, not clear which of the two directions should be ascribed to this effect. These comprise the Late Cretaceous E1 Rio tonalite pluton, the Eocene pyroxene diorite intrusion of LaJina and the Late Miocene andesite prophyry intrusive of Las Yayas de Viajama (Fig. 1). According to available geological information (BOwIN, 1966: MACDONALD and MELSON, 1969; PALMER, 1972; LEWIS, 1977), none of these units appear to have been structurally deformed and the first two are quite fresh, while the andesite is somewhat weathered in exposures in elevated positions, but not in stream beds. th the Mississippi Valley group of ores as a whole, the ores occur in dolostones and, only to a minor extent, in equally porous and permeable sandstones. Also, fluid inclusion studies have shown repeatedly that the Mississippi Valley-type ores were probably deposited from low-temperature, high-sa- linity brines (Roedder, 1967, 1977a and b). The Vi- burnum mines, regionally and locally, are structurally high and on the flanks of a major sedimentary basin in a cratonic setting. The ore is stratabound, confined to the Upper Cainbrian Bonneterre Dolostone, and of simple mineralogy, consisting predominantly of galena, sphalerite, marcasite, and pyrite. The mines are largely associated with drapes over highs of the hummocky Precambrian basement or within strati- graphic traps adjacent to monoclinal dips to the west- erly trending basin. The lead isotopes are complex and have been regarded as derived from sedimentary sources (Doe and Delevaux, 1972, Sverjensky et al., 1979). Sulfur isotopes show a wide spread and are likewise considered to be derived from sedimentary sources, probably from sulfate deposited within more restricted facies of the Bonneterre host rock. The Haukivesi area The Haukivesi area is located in the south- eastern part of the Raahe—Ladoga zone (Fig. 1). The geology of the area has been described in detail by Hackman (1933), Gaål and Rauha- mäki (1971) and Korsman and Pääjärvi (1980). The area is characterized by highly meta- morphic supracrustal rocks and by hyper- sthene-bearing plutonic rocks with sporadic basic (subsilicic) dykes (Fig. 2). The subracrustal complex consists of garnet-cordierite-sillimanite gneisses, hyper- sthene gneisses and hypersthene amphib- olites. The garnet-cordierite-sillimanite gneisses are migmatized by trondhjemites. The metamorphism of these rocks took place under conditions of granulite facies but, according to Paavola (1976), the pressure was not very high during the recrystallization. Agglomeratic and pillow lava structures in some of the amphibolites and gneisses in the area suggest a volcanic origin for these rocks. The remanent magnetization found in these 112 K. J. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. The width of the dykes varies from a few centi- metres to about 150 metres. The contacts be- tween the diabase and the wall rock are always very sharp, and chilled margins are usual. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. The Haukivesi area The Haukivesi area is located in the south- eastern part of the Raahe—Ladoga zone (Fig. 1). The geology of the area has been described in detail by Hackman (1933), Gaål and Rauha- mäki (1971) and Korsman and Pääjärvi (1980). The area is characterized by highly meta- morphic supracrustal rocks and by hyper- sthene-bearing plutonic rocks with sporadic basic (subsilicic) dykes (Fig. 2). The subracrustal complex consists of garnet-cordierite-sillimanite gneisses, hyper- sthene gneisses and hypersthene amphib- olites. The metamorphism of these rocks took place under conditions of granulite facies but, according to Paavola (1976), the pressure was not very high during the recrystallization. Closer to the Bothnian Sea, at the north- western end of the Belt metamorphism has taken place mainly under conditions of am- phibolite facies. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. The width of the dykes varies from a few centi- metres to about 150 metres. The contacts be- tween the diabase and the wall rock are always very sharp, and chilled margins are usual. Paleomagnetic data on the Main Sulphide Ore Belt in Finland are coherent but differ clearly from those obtained on the Archean basement area immediately north of it. The coherent magnetization in ithe Belt could have been caused by (i) axial uplift, (ii) a plate suture along the Belt or (iii) a short-time igneous pulse. The last interpretation is accepted since it agrees with the radiometric age data. Thus the paleomagnetic measurements in the area date the same thermal events as do the radiometric U-Pb age determinations, and the shape of the APW curve is thereby verified. A paleomagnetic pole determined for dykes intersecting the Archean basement block lies off the accepted APW curve which possibly need to be corrected. Paleomagnetic data on the Main Sulphide Ore Belt in Finland are coherent but differ clearly from those obtained on the Archean basement area immediately north of it. The coherent magnetization in ithe Belt could have been caused by (i) axial uplift, (ii) a plate suture along the Belt or (iii) a short-time igneous pulse. The last interpretation is accepted since it agrees with the radiometric age data. Thus the paleomagnetic measurements in the area date the same thermal events as do the radiometric U-Pb age determinations, and the shape of the APW curve is thereby verified. A paleomagnetic pole determined for dykes intersecting the Archean basement block lies off the accepted APW curve which possibly need to be corrected. The magmatic pulse between 1880— 1840 Ma may have been associated with a plate collision or with a deep fluid convection producing the sulphide ore precipitation within the Belt. K. J. The paleomagnetic mea- surements are concentrated on two areas: One is in the central part of the Main Sul- phide Ore Belt in the Haukivesi area, the other is just north of the Belt in the Archean basement complex in the Nilsiä—Varpais- järvi area (Fig. 1). The lithology and paleo- magnetic data obtained will be described and discussed below. Additional paleomagnetic results already available from the north- western end of the Belt and from the Iisalmi area (see Fig. 1) will be included in the Dis- cussion. Radiometric age data and lead iso- tope values will also be considered in drawing conclusions about the origin and evolution of the Belt. The lithology of the area Lithologically, the Belt is not well defined and its borders cannot be drawn exactly. It consists of series of metasediments and meta- volcanics deformed, recrystallized and folded during the Svecokarelian (1800—1900 Ma) orogeny. These schists and gneisses are pene- trated by various of intrusive rocks mainly of synkinematic character. An area typical of the Belt is met with in the southeastern part of the zone in the Haukivesi area (Figs. 1 and 2). Denmark, vol. 30, pp. 57-67. Copenhagen, November 12th, 1981. Pseudotachylite veins from the northern margin of the Ikertoq shear belt possess a highly-stable rema- nence residing in magnetite. Sites in seven veins define a mean axis of magnetisation D = 269°, I = 22° (k=23) with one vein possessing opposite polarity to the remainder. The palaeomagnetic results show that brittle fracture events represented by the pseudotachylites occurred during a single episode. Similar directions of magnetisation in some of the kimberlite-lamprophyre dykes intruding the Ikertoq belt demonstrate a close temporal relationship between the pseudotachylites and the earlier part of the (c. 580 Ma) kimberlite/lamprophyre magmatism. Alternating field and thermal demagnetisation studies of lavas and sediments assigned to the Proterozoic Jotnian of western Sweden (Dalarna) and eastern Norway are reported. Hematite is the predominant remanence carrier in the sediments. These locally record a dipolar axis of magnetisation D= 14" and I = 10". but the bulk of the sediments, including the western part of the outcrop and all of the upper sequence, have a characteristic remanence ca. D= 160", 1=35". interpreted as a magnetic overprint during the Sveconorwegian mobile episode (1 100-800 hla). The lavas have low deuteric oxidation states but were subjected to widespread hematisation during later hydrothermal activity.

Discussion of results Six sites from Jotnian hematite-bearing sedi- ments of this study define a dipolar axis of magnetisation D= 14", I= lo", and eight sites from the lavas define a mean D = 4", I = -2". We believe that these directions define the geomagnetic field axes at the time of deutenc- hydrothermal alteration of the lavas and deposi- tion-lithifcation of the sediments, because (1) they include directions of both polarities, (2) it is the only coherent direction recovered from the lavas, and (3) it includes the lavas subjected to minimal alteration. In addition, these directions reside in hematite at some sites and in magnetite at others. sequence (Fig. I) comprises an un- known number of amygdaloidal and (sometimes) porphyritic olivine basalt flows, which are lo- cally scoriaceous or pillowy (Hjelmqvist 1966). They are composed of an ophitic groundmass of labradorite or bytownite feldspar surrounding pseudomorphs of sericite, chlorite and ores after olivine and augite; vesicles are filled with hydrothermal epidote, calcite, chalcedony or chlorite. The Jotnian sequence is extensively cut by (‘post-Jotnian’) dolerites mostly in the form of sills and thick SE-NW dykes; these are fresh ophitic dolerites comprising labradorite feldspar, augite, olivine, ilmenite and magnetite. They have been the subject of extensive RbSr studies by Patchett (1978) who has derived ages of 1232-1228 Ma (Idre), 1217 Ma (Mossiberg), 1247 Ma (BornSssjon), I23 1 Ma (Alvdalslsen), 1223 Ma (Emidden) and 1290-1215 Ma (Alvho); they have a comparable age and magnetisation to the extensive post-Jotnian dolerites of eastern Swe- den and Finland (Patchett et al. 1978; Piper 1979). Under favourable circumstances these may yield essen- tially instantaneous records of the geomagnetic field and (in the latter case) place this informa- tion in a time sequence. Real progress in under- standing the Precambrian geomagnetic field is hampered by the paucity of suitable volcanic andlor sedimentary suites. Studies to date on the ca. 1100 Ma Keweenawan lavas of North America (eg. Palmer 1970) and the ca. 1300 Ma Gardar lavas of Greenland (Piper 1977) have recovered a primary remanence and a sequence of magnetic field reversals. (All ages quoted in this paper have been recalculated to the decay constants listed by Steiger & Jager [ 19771.) This paper reports a comparable study of the Jotnian lavas and sediments of western Sweden and eastern Norway. Geology and age The term 'Jotnian' (Sederholm 1927; von Eck- ermann 1937) is used to embrace the sedimentary and volcanic suites within the Fen- noscandian Shield post-dating the last Pre- cambrian mobile episode. Real progress in under- standing the Precambrian geomagnetic field is hampered by the paucity of suitable volcanic andlor sedimentary suites. The dolerites of the main part of the Sarv Nappe contain, after progressive alternating field and thermal demagnetization, a stable magnetic component of decl. 21.4". incl. -9.1". ass= 12.4'. k= 11.3. This gives a geomagnetic pole at lat. 21"N, long. 170"E which is in agreement with published Silurian-Devonian poles from Fennoscandia. This together with a simple 'fold test' implies that the Proterozoic dolerites became remagnetized during the Caledonian orogeny. Palaeomagnetism has had its main success in establishing the presence of large-scale move- ments in the Earth's crust but the method is also applicable in many other fields such as the study of events in a period of orogeny. For example, the measurements of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), can give information about the magnetization build-up in relation to the metamorphic history of different units, in- cluding studies of relative movements. The Geotraverse, from Ostersund in Sweden across the Scandinavian Caledonides to Trondheim in Norway (Annersten 1973; Bylund et al. 1976) presents numerous possibilities for studies of this kind, and an obvious subject for such work is the well preserved parts of the Sarv Nappe with its conspicuous swarm of tholeiitic dolerite dykes. Very little is at present understood about conti- nental movements and the behaviour of the Earth's magnetic field in Cambrian times, and such data as are presently available suggest that large apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) movements characterised this period (Bucha 1%5; Mc- Elhinny et al. 1974; Moms & Roy 1977). The pre- sent paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of the Alnon Complex falling within this general objec- tive. All radiometric ages quoted have been recalculated using the new decay constants re- commended by IUGS (Steiger & Jager 1977). Age of the Alnon Complex The Alnon Complex comprises a suite of alkaline plutonic rocks ranging from pyroxenite to ijolite- melteigite and nepheline syenite in composi- tion. They are surrounded by a fenite aureole, and cut by sovite ring-dykes. The main intrusion at Alnon Island is accompanied by several satel- lite intrusions: Bdrang (sovite), Salskar (brec- cia), Sordker (melilite-rich rocks) and possibly Avike Bay (sovite?). Two important tectonic lineaments intersect in Scania (SkAne), southernmost Sweden. One is the zone separating the Precambrian Fennoscan- dian Shield from central Europe and its sedimentary cover and the other is the Protogine Zone (PZ) which constitutes the border between the entirely different Proterozoic terrains of the southwestern and central Fennoscandian Shield. Movements and intrusions in these zones have contributed to the mosaic pattern and the mix of Proterozoic gneisses, granites and Phanerozoic sediments that form the geology of Scania. The purpose of this paper is to present a study of the magnetic properties of intrusive hyperite doler- ites and syenites from the Scanian part of the PZ in relation to their situation in the intersection between those tectonic lineaments. The Protogine Zone - other names sometimes used for this feature are the Schistosity Zone, The Gothide Front, the Svecononvegian Front - trends from Scania northwards across southern Sweden to Nonvay where it is cut by the Scan- dinavian Caledonides (Fig. 1). It separates the Svecononvegian southwestern corner of the Fennsocandian Shield from its central Sveco- karelian part. There is at present a running discussion whether the PZ is part of a global suture, the scar of a plate collision between a "Grenvillian-Svecononvegian" plate 'and the Laurentian-Fennoscandian plate or whether it is an intrashield structure along which movements have occurred intermittently during the Precam- brian, i.e. Donaldson et al. (19731, Zeck & Malling (l976), Patchett & Bylund (l977), Piper (1980), Gorbatschev (1980). and Lindh et al. (in press). INTRODUCTION Little palaeomagnetic work has been done on Palaeozoic rocks in Tasmania. The only published palaeomagnetic study of the Tasmanian Ordovician is by Briden (1967), who found that,the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of certain Lower Ordovician sandstones represented a secondary magnetization. Briden regarded this as resulting from regional heating during the Tertiary. The limestones in the Ida Bay region of southern Tasmania are amongst the least folded and the least altered Ordovician rocks in Tasmania. It was hoped, therefore, that they would retain a primary magnetization, thus allowing the determination of the palaeolatitude of _Tasmania at the time of limestone deposition. This study was initially undertaken by one of the authors (C.S.) as part of a broader sedimentological study of Ordovician rocks in the Ida Bay area. The laboratory work in this project was undertaken at the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Australian National University in Canberra. ABSTRACT The paleomagnetic analysis of samples from the lower Permian Paso Hondo y Grupera Forma­ tions, collected near Chicomuselo, Chiapas, yields an equatorial latitude and implies that the sampling area was in a position rotated 22° counterclockwise relative to cratonic North Amer­ ica. By contrast, the poleposition obtained from the Pennsylvanian-Permian Yododeiie Forma­ tion, collected near Nochixtlan, Oaxaca, closely agrees with equivalent North American data. This implies that the Isthmus of Tchuantepec represents a major discontinuity. The sites were chosen from aerial photographic maps and from geological maps kindly made available to us by Mooser. LABORATORY PROCEDURES Samples were obtained with a hand corer. They were oriented by means of a mag­ netic inclinometer and in some cases additionally with a sun-compass. From each site 2 or 3 pilot-specimens were demagnetized in an increasing alternating field to get the range of field strengths, at which the palaeomagnetic directions were most stable. This range was determined using Zijdetveld diagrams and a stability index according to Symons and Stupavsky ( 1974). The other specimens were demagne­ tized in alternating fields within this stable range. A Digico spinner magnetometer was used to determine the magnetization. Demagnetization was carried out with a Schonstedt af-demagnetizer and, above 80 kA/m ( 1000 Oe ), with a tumbler appa­ ratus. Some samples were thermally demagnetized using a Schonstedt apparatus; their mag11etization was measured with a Czechoslovakian JR-3 spinner magneto­ meter. Las rocas {gneas estudiadas son del Plioceno y Cuaternario, con la excepcion del macizo de Palma Sola, de edad Mioceno. Los resultados paleomagneticos se usan para correlacionar con resultados geoqu{micos y geologicos del area y con resultados paleomagneticos de Norteamerica y Mexico. Los resultados no indican movimiento relativo signiflcante entre Norteamerica y la seccion cen­ tral-este de Mexico en el periodo estudiado. ABSTRACT About 500 oriented samples were taken from 59 sites in the eastern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt. The investigated igneous rocks are of Pliocene to Quaternary, and additionally in the Palma Sola Massif of Miocene age. Besides correlations with geochemical and geological results it was the intention to determine the mean poles from the palaeomagnetic directions for the Quaternary and upper Tertiary. Starting from reconstructions of the continental drift as e.g. the well known "Bullard-fit", Mexico obviously could not have been part of the North American plate in former times, as this would imply large overlapping with South America. Therefore, several models were proposed which allow Mexico to arrive at the today position by movements along different postulated shear zones (e.g. Dickinson and Coney, 1980; Gose et al., 1980). Most authors assume that the main movement occurred soon after the opening of the Atlantic. Other researchers assume movements until Tertiary times (e.g. Walper, 1980). Some palaeomagnetic results seem to support this idea (Urrutia-Fucugauchi and Pal, 1977; Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981 b) as well as the concept of microplate ro­ tations near the TMVB (Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981a). Samples were, therefore, taken from the eastern part of the TMVB, dating back to the upper Tertiary, to examine if such movements could be detected in this region. They were oriented by means of a mag­ netic inclinometer and in some cases additionally with a sun-compass. From each site 2 or 3 pilot-specimens were demagnetized in an increasing alternating field to get the range of field strengths, at which the palaeomagnetic directions were most stable. This range was determined using Zijdetveld diagrams and a stability index according to Symons and Stupavsky ( 1974). The other specimens were demagne­ tized in alternating fields within this stable range. A Digico spinner magnetometer was used to determine the magnetization. Demagnetization was carried out with a Schonstedt af-demagnetizer and, above 80 kA/m ( 1000 Oe ), with a tumbler appa­ ratus. Some samples were thermally demagnetized using a Schonstedt apparatus; their mag11etization was measured with a Czechoslovakian JR-3 spinner magneto­ meter. Los resultados paleomagneticos se usan para correlacionar con resultados geoqu{micos y geologicos del area y con resultados paleomagneticos de Norteamerica y Mexico. Los resultados no indican movimiento relativo signiflcante entre Norteamerica y la seccion cen­ tral-este de Mexico en el periodo estudiado. ABSTRACT About 500 oriented samples were taken from 59 sites in the eastern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt. The investigated igneous rocks are of Pliocene to Quaternary, and additionally in the Palma Sola Massif of Miocene age. Besides correlations with geochemical and geological results it was the intention to determine the mean poles from the palaeomagnetic directions for the Quaternary and upper Tertiary. The work included aerial-photography interpretation, mapping and sampling for geochemical investiga­ tions and radiometric datings. Also in 1980; about 500 oriented samples were taken for palaeomagnetic work. Besides special investigations in conjunction with the geochemical and geological investigations it was the aim of those measurements to obtain new data for the secular variation of the earth's magnetic field at this lati­ tude, as well as to search for possible tectonic motions between the sampling area and North America. The plate tectonic evolution of Mexico is still unknown because only 3: few re­ liable palaeomagnetic data are available today. Starting from reconstructions of the continental drift as e.g. the well known "Bullard-fit", Mexico obviously could not have been part of the North American plate in former times, as this would imply large overlapping with South America. Therefore, several models were proposed which allow Mexico to arrive at the today position by movements along different postulated shear zones (e.g. Dickinson and Coney, 1980; Gose et al., 1980). Most authors assume that the main movement occurred soon after the opening of the Atlantic. Other researchers assume movements until Tertiary times (e.g. Walper, 1980). Some palaeomagnetic results seem to support this idea (Urrutia-Fucugauchi and Pal, 1977; Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981 b) as well as the concept of microplate ro­ tations near the TMVB (Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981a). OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian. Lava locally ascended along these tectonic lines towards the surface. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian.

An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian. Lava locally ascended along these tectonic lines towards the surface. This period was succeeded by an intense peneplana- tion, at which time clastic rocks were being deposited while the climate changed from humid to arid. Thick sediments layers were accumulated in the Lower Permian (Autunian, Saxonian). In Upper Permian (Thuringian), after other tectonic movements, rocks were deposited especially in deltas. Triassic sediments developed under quite different conditions [1]. A vast depression filled with water of marine nature was formed over the entire territory of western Bulgaria. Since the Variscan mountain system was already a peneplane, equal sedimentation conditions prevailed not only in the study area but also far to the NE and SW. A systematic paleomagnetic study has been made of Permian greenstones and asso- ciated sediments from the inner belt of central Japan. The greenstones are generally meta- morpho

aleomagnetic study has been made of Permian greenstones and asso- ciated sediments from the inner belt of central Japan. The greenstones are generally meta- morphosed into the zeolite facies to greenschist facies grade. The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization of the greenstones decreases with increase of metamorphic grade toward the greenschist facies. Metamorphism as low or lower than the greenschist facies grade does not create chemical remanent magnetization in the greenstones. Reliable mag- netic directions were obtained from the greenstones and associated sediments occurring in the lowest grade metamorphic zones after thermal demagnetization and alternating field demagnetization. After correction of the magnetic directions with respect to the folding axes and bedding planes, the Permian magnetic inclination in Japan was deduced yielding the suggestion that Japan was situated in an equatorial region in the late Paleozoic period, perhaps as part of a missing continent, Pacifica. Since then, the Far East microplate including Japan migrated toward the north, and collided with the Asian mainland in the late Mesozoic. INTRODUCTION Many paleomagnetic studies have been made on late Mesozoic and Ceno- zoic rocks in Japan, and Yaskawa and Nakajima (1974) have summarized the avai

d in central Japan (Hattori and Hirooka, 1977). But, the data are too few to allow any conclu- sion to be drawn and systematic studies of Paleozoic paleomagnetism are necessary to delineate the drift path of Japan and to gain a better under- standing of the paleogeography relevant to Japan in Paleozoic time. The systematic paleomagnetic study described in this paper has been directed toward the lower to middle Permian greenstones of the northern part of the inner belt of central Japan (Fig. 1). The metamorphic grade in this region is generally low and the greenstones have been comparatively well preserved. The geology and greenstone petrography of the Fujibashi and the central and western Nanjo areas are the subject of ongoing investigation by the present authors. Taking field and petrographic evidence into account, we have been able to obtaine reliable paleomagnetic records from the green- stones. In this paper, the relationship between metamorphism and magneti- zation is elucidated and paleomagnetic data for the Permian paleolatitude of Japan are presented. 213 GEOLOGIC SETTING AND GREENSTONE PETROGRAPHY For this study, 39 sites in the Wakasa, western Nanjo, central Nanjo, and Fujibashi areas were visited, and total collection represents 35 sites of green- stone, two

etic study has been made of Permian greenstones and asso- ciated sediments from the inner belt of central Japan. The greenstones are generally meta- morphosed into the zeolite facies to greenschist facies grade. The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization of the greenstones decreases with increase of metamorphic grade toward the greenschist facies. Metamorphism as low or lower than the greenschist facies grade does not create chemical remanent magnetization in the greenstones. Reliable mag- netic directions were obtained from the greenstones and associated sediments occurring in the lowest grade metamorphic zones after thermal demagnetization and alternating field demagnetization. After correction of the magnetic directions with respect to the folding axes and bedding planes, the Permian magnetic inclination in Japan was deduced yielding the suggestion that Japan was situated in an equatorial region in the late Paleozoic period, perhaps as part of a missing continent, Pacifica. Since then, the Far East microplate including Japan migrated toward the north, and collided with the Asian mainland in the late Mesozoic. Paleomagnetic evidence for non-Apenninic origin of the Sila nappes (Calabria). Tectonophysics, 60: 169-188 The magnetization of Lower Permian rocks from Sila has a mean direction D = 56.5’, I = +20.4’ with ogs = 9.1’ after correction for Upper Neogene tilting. A further correc- tion for the attitude of the nappes after their Middle Miocene emplacement establishes paleolatitudes consistent with those from the Lower Permian Tethys. The remarkable internal consistency of the data has not supported the distinction of units with opposite vergences within the Sila crystalline nappes. The declination indicates that the Sila massif has rotated counter-clockwise by about 90’ relative to the Apennines, Sardinia and the Southern Alps and therefore the well-known Apenninic rotation alone does not account for the total change of direction in tectonic transport. Accordingly, the structural trends of tectonic phases older than the emplacement time of the Calabrian nappes should no longer be referred to present-day geographic coordinates. The post-Late Cretaceous motion relative to the north Calabrian Apennines enhances the geotectonic role of the northern boundary of the Calab

ues in the interpretation of the structure of the Mediterranean. The Sangineto line marks its northern boundary in Calabria and the Taor- mina line marks its southern boundary in Sicily; both lines have been assumed by diverging modern interpretations to represent the Africa- Europe boundary. THE TECTONIC SETTING The allochthonous character of all the exposed pre-Miocene rocks piled up in complex nappes is now generally accepted. The occurrence among them 170 of nappes with Hercynian plutonites and metamorphic rocks (Calabride units by Ogniben, 1969) has fostered divergent speculations on the original loca- tion, the history of deformation, and the transport of the fragmented con- tinental crust. In recent interpretations some models consider all structures as originally belonging to an Apenninic domain or geo-syncline with most, but not all, directions of transport from the west (e.g. Ogniben, 1969). Dubois, 1976 and other authors assume that a north-African chain was fragmented, deformed and displaced by the Europe-Africa collision. Micro- plate models advocate the drifting of the entire crust of Calabria from a frag- mented Alpine belt east of Sardinia, in spite of the known allochthony of all exposed terreins and of the lack of information on the nature of the bas

tion, the history of deformation, and the transport of the fragmented con- tinental crust. In recent interpretations some models consider all structures as originally belonging to an Apenninic domain or geo-syncline with most, but not all, directions of transport from the west (e.g. Ogniben, 1969). Dubois, 1976 and other authors assume that a north-African chain was fragmented, deformed and displaced by the Europe-Africa collision. Micro- plate models advocate the drifting of the entire crust of Calabria from a frag- mented Alpine belt east of Sardinia, in spite of the known allochthony of all exposed terreins and of the lack of information on the nature of the base- ment (Alvarez et al., 1974). When units from an Alpine chain are considered as the source of the upper nappes with Hercynian rocks, such as the Sila nappes, coming to override the structures of the Apenninic chain, different phases of directions of transport are required. According to Haccard et al. (1972): there was first an Alp-Apennine compression, then tectonic transport from the east, and subsequently Apen- ninic transport from the west, the southwest and the south. According to Mascle and Grandjacquet (1978), Cretaceous transport from the south or southeast and east was followed by Upper Cretaceous

erms of present geography; in the second case, directions are chosen according to the requirements of the pro- posed models. The complexities of the interpretations stem from an extrem- ely intricate geologic history. Amodio Morelli et al. (1976) have made an interpretative review of models put forward to explain the origin of the Calabrian-Peloritan arc. In this reconstruction the Alpine nappes with vergence toward Europe overrode Apenninic terrain with southeasterly and easterly vergence toward the African foreland during the Miocene. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. A number of structural-stratigraphic units may be defined (Figs. 2 and 3). These units are geological bodies which display homogeneity in facies and tectonic behaviour, and are derived from pre-existing palaeogeographic units. Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. A number of structural-stratigraphic units may be defined (Figs. 2 and 3). These units are geological bodies which display homogeneity in facies and tectonic behaviour, and are derived from pre-existing palaeogeographic units. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. As in certain previous studies of the Periadriatic Scaglia limestones, alternating field demagnetization techniques were sufficient to produce a stable characteristic magnetization for the white and pink Scaglia (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975, 1977) but thermal techniques were necessary in the case of the red (Roggenthen and Napoleone, 1977; Channel1 et al., 1979). The precise age of the Late Cretaceous Scaglia was not palaeontologically ascertained for all sampling sites. Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. A number of structural-stratigraphic units may be defined (Figs. 2 and 3). These units are geological bodies which display homogeneity in facies and tectonic behaviour, and are derived from pre-existing palaeogeographic units. This paper reports the work of a small joint expedition from the Australian National University and Macquarie University, which, in the 1968-1969 summer season, set out to determine whether bending had occurred and the structural implications of such movements. Tec- tonophysics, 63 : 97-90. Palaeomagnetic determinations for Jurassic volcanics and a Cretaceous quartz-dolerite sill at three localities around the arcuate Patagonian Cordillera show that a bending of 40” to 27” has occurred. Since the structural bend is 90° it is probable that the Mesozoic arc was originally curved. Cainozoic dykes and sills at Lago San Martin in the northward- trending belt and Sierra Valdivieso in the eastward-trending belt have the same magnetic directions and were intruded after bending. These results essentially confirm the palaeomagnetic determinations of Dalziel et al., (1973a) and further suggest that the collapse of the marginal sea during the Late Cretaceous orogenesis resulted in greater bending in the outer arc than in the inner arc. The orocline must have formed during the Andean orogeny between 80 m.y. and 21 m.y. ago and was accompanied by folding and thrusting. INTRODUCTION Sulawesi consists of two major tectonic units, namely an eastern arc, dominated by thrust tectonics in connection with emplacement of an exten- sive ophiolite sequence, and a western arc, characterized by normal folding, widespread Cenozoic volcanism and granite intrusions. Many hypotheses on the tectonic history of Sulawesi have so far been put forward to account for the complex geological and geophysical features of the island. The most noteworthy are those by Katili (1975, 1978), Audley- Charles et al. (1972) and Audley-Charles (1974). The authors have suggested in these publications that their ideas should be confirmed by paleomagnetic 164 methods before being considered established. (1972). One of the main purposes of our studies is to offer a tectonic framework for the western arc of Sulawesi from the paleomagnetic view point. Recon- naissance paleomagnetic investigations combined with fission-track age dating were carried out by us in southwest Sulawesi (Biru area), central Sulawesi (Gimpu and Megapa) and north Sulawesi (Kampong Kombi and Tansealama). DISCUSSION From Table III and Fig. 2 it appears that since the Middle Miocene (13 m.y. B.P.) to Recent all the VGP’s significantly group about the present north pole, suggesting that the paleomagnetic pole position is consistent with the present north pole within the range of errors. Contrary to this, the VGP’s for pre-Middle Miocene rocks show a fairly scattered distribution. It may be very difficult to derive a reliable unique explanation of the paleomagnetic features based on these scattered groupings of VGP’s. Needless to say, such a divergence of the VGP’s cannot be reconciled merely with polar wandering and paleosecular variation for the period concerned. INTRODUCTION Sulawesi consists of two major tectonic units, namely an eastern arc, dominated by thrust tectonics in connection with emplacement of an exten- sive ophiolite sequence, and a western arc, characterized by normal folding, widespread Cenozoic volcanism and granite intrusions. Many hypotheses on the tectonic history of Sulawesi have so far been put forward to account for the complex geological and geophysical features of the island. The most noteworthy are those by Katili (1975, 1978), Audley- Charles et al. (1972) and Audley-Charles (1974). The authors have suggested in these publications that their ideas should be confirmed by paleomagnetic 164 methods before being considered established. on a reconnaissance paleomagnetic survey in southwest and southeast Sulawesi, Haile (1978) found evidence to support quite separate paleogeographic positions of these two regions at the Early Cretaceous period, as postulated originally by Audley-Charles et al. (1972). One of the main purposes of our studies is to offer a tectonic framework for the western arc of Sulawesi from the paleomagnetic view point. Recon- naissance paleomagnetic investigations combined with fission-track age dating were carried out by us in southwest Sulawesi (Biru area), central Sulawesi (Gimpu and Megapa) and north Sulawesi (Kampong Kombi and Tansealama). Sample localities are shown in Fig. 1. The geologic setting of these three regions will be described in the following section. Most rock samples (eighteen sites) were collected from the Biru area, as for this area a detailed geological map was available. As can be seen from Fig. 1, three of the sample localities occur close two prominent fault zones, the Watampone fault and Palu-Koro strike-slip fault (Tjia and Zakaria, 1974), and therefore special care was taken to collect undisturbed rock samples. lt. 165 GEOLOGIC SETTING Southwest Sulawesi Regional mapping of south Sulawesi has been carried out by the Geologi- cal Survey of Indonesia (Sukamto, 1975). The Biru area was investigated in detail during a mineral survey by Rio Tinto Indonesia (Van Leeuwen, 1975). Its generalized stratigraphy and the sampling horizons are shown in Table I. The oldest rocks of South Sulawesi are basement complexes of polymeta- morphic rocks, which are unconformably overlain by Lower Cretaceous deep-sea sediments. These in turn are unconformably overlain by a series of Upper Cretaceous shale, greywacke and arkose with interbedded volcanics (Marada Sandstone). After a period of folding and erosion, a NNW trending talc-alkaline vol- canic chain (Langi volcanics) developed during the Paleocene.
